3586.t: Perhaps from λέπω (lépō, “to peel”) + -ις (-ĭs, feminine suffix).

3510.t: Traditionally considered a metathesis from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb- (“hazy, deep”), with cognates including Old Church Slavonic дъно (dŭno), Old English dēop (English deep) and Albanian det (from Proto-Albanian *deubeta).

3500.t: From αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) + Proto-Hellenic *mətós, from Proto-Indo-European *mn̥tós, from *men- (“to think”) (whence μένος (ménos) and others).

3569.t: From κριτήρ (krĭtḗr, “interpreter”) + -ιον (-ĭon), from κρίνω (krī́nō, “I discern, judge”).

3571.t: From κτίζω (ktízō, “to found, to build”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

3511.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gʷə́lanos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂- (“acorn”); see there for cognates. Probably unrelated to Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (bălăneîon, “bath, bathroom”).

3565.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kónh₂m (“leg”); cognate with English ham (from Proto-Germanic *hammō) and Old Irish cnáim (“bone”).

3578.t: According to Beekes, of Pre-Greek origin, based on the lack of a clear root and corresponding verb to which the word would trace back to, as well as similarities to words like κώδεια (kṓdeia, “poppyhead”), which suggest a substrate borrowing.

3505.t: Probably Pre-Greek. Has been compared to βαίνω (baínō, “to go, move”), but Beekes finds this unconvincing.

3579.t: Likely from the root of λαγαρός (lăgărós, “hollow; slack”).

3501.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂emǵʰ-w-eh₁-n, from *h₂énǵʰus (“narrow, tight”), and compared in particular to Old Armenian օձիք (ōjikʻ, “collar”), though this is controversial.

3531.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dusmenḗs, from Proto-Indo-European *dusmenēs (whence also Sanskrit दुर्मनस् (durmanas), Avestan 𐬛𐬎𐬱𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵 (dušmanah), Middle Persian [script needed] (dwšmn'), Middle Persian [script needed] (dwšmyn'), Manichaean Middle Persian 𐫅𐫇𐫢𐫖𐫏𐫗…

3507.t: From βίος (bíos) + -όω (-óō). Doublet of inherited ζῶ (zô).

3509.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mləspʰāmos, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥-s-bʰeh₂-mo-s, from *(s)mel- (“to deceive”) + φημί (phēmí, “to say”) + -ος (-os, adjective-forming suffix).

3503.t: Related to the comparative βελτίων (beltíōn), with the suffix -ιστος (-istos).

3502.t: Compared with Lithuanian vilkti (“to drag, haul”) and Proto-Slavic *velťi (“to draw”). Beekes claims that the variants point to a Pre-Greek origin, in particular a form *alʷ-ak-.

3512.t: From Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare), from Demotic Egyptian br, from Egyptian bꜣjr (“transport ship”), b-bA-A-y:r*Z1-P1

3572.t: Often connected with Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“to crook, bend”) (whence perhaps κυλλός (kullós, “crooked”)), but Beekes doesn't find this convincing.

3597.t: From the root of μῆρα (mêra) and μηρός (mērós).

3589.t: Unexplained. Maybe from Old Persian *merdum gija (“plant of humans”), but it could be a folk-etymological adaptation of a foreign word.

3599.t: From a Semitic source; compare Hebrew מגדל (migdál, “tower”) and Akkadian 𒈠𒀜𒂵𒆷𒌅 (madgaltu, “watchtower”); for further etymology and connections see Arabic مِجْدَل (mijdal).

3568.t: Derived from a nominal base form, like κνημίς (knēmī́s) and χειρίς (kheirī́s), or perhaps this word just took over their ending; the technical meaning suggests a loan.

3588.t: From λυπέω (lūpéō, “to grieve”) + -ρός (-rós). Compare also λυπρός (lūprós).

3541.t: Unknown, though note also θλίβω (thlíbō, “to squeeze, distress”) and φλάω (phláō, “to crush, bruise”). Not related to θλάσπις (thlắspĭs, “shepherd's purse”), despite folk etymological linkage.

3582.t: Likely from λᾶς (lâs, contracted form of λᾶας (lâăs, “stone”)) + *ξεύω (*xeúō, unattested variant of ξέω (xéō, “to smooth; to polish”)).

3566.t: Back-formation from κοινωνέω (koinōnéō), after pairs like στρατηγέω (stratēgéō) and στρατηγός (stratēgós).
